entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11159"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.13.1-Ezek.13.23">Eze 13:1-23</reference>. Denunciation of False Prophets and Prophetesses; Their False Teachings, and God's Consequent Judgments.</title> <div sID="gen20118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11159"/>1. As the twelfth chapter denounced the false expectations of the people, so this denounces the false leaders who fed those expectations. As an independent witness, Ezekiel confirms at the Chebar the testimony of Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">Jr 29:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.31">31</reference>) in his letter from Jerusalem to the captive exiles, against the false prophets; of these some were conscious knaves, others fanatical dupes of their own frauds; for example, Ahab, Zedekiah, and Shemaiah. Hananiah must have believed his own lie, else he would not have specified so circumstantial details (<reference osisRef="Jer.28.2-Jer.28.4">Jr 28:2-4</reference>). The conscious knaves gave only general assurances of peace (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jr 5:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">14:13</reference>). The language of Ezekiel has plain references to the similar language of Jeremiah (for example, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.9-Jer.23.38">Jr 23:9-38</reference>); the bane of false prophecy, which had its stronghold in Jerusalem, having in some degree extended to the Chebar; this chapter, therefore, is primarily intended as a message to those still in the Jewish metropolis; and, secondarily, for the good of the exiles at the Chebar. <div eID="gen20118" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11160"/><div sID="gen20119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11160"/><hi type="bold">2. that prophesy--</hi>namely, a speedy return to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen20119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of ... own hearts--</hi>alluding to the words of Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.16">Jr 23:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.26">26</reference>); that is, what they prophesied was what they and the people wished; the wish was father to the thought. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11161"/><div sID="gen20121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11161"/><hi type="bold">3. foolish--</hi>though vaunting as though exclusively possessing "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19-1Cor.1.21">1Co 1:19-21</reference>); the fear of God being the only beginning of wisdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference>).<div eID="gen20121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own spirit--</hi>instead of the Spirit of God. A threefold distinction lay between the false and the true prophets: (1) The source of their messages respectively; of the false, "their own hearts"; of the true, an object presented to the spiritual sense (named from the noblest of the senses, a seeing) by the Spirit of God as from without, not produced by their own natural powers of reflection. The word, the body of the thought, presented itself not audibly to the natural sense, but directly to the spirit of the prophet; and so the perception of it is properly called a seeing, he perceiving that which thereafter forms itself in his soul as the cover of the external word [Delitzsch]; hence the peculiar expression, "seeing the word of God" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">Is 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1">13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>) The point aimed at; the false "walking after their own spirit"; the true, after the Spirit of God. (3) The result; the false saw nothing, but spake as if they had seen; the true had a vision, not subjective, but objectively real [Fairbairn]. A refutation of those who set the inward word above the objective, and represent the Bible as flowing subjectively from the inner light of its writers, not from the revelation of the Holy Ghost from without. "They are impatient to get possession of the kernel without its fostering shell--they would have Christ without the Bible" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen20122" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11162"/><div sID="gen20123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11162"/><hi type="bold">4. foxes--</hi>which cunningly "spoil the vines" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.15">So 2:15</reference>), Israel being the vineyard (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.15">Psa 80:8-15</reference>; Is 5:1-7; 27:2; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jr 2:21</reference>); their duty was to have guarded it from being spoiled, whereas they themselves spoiled it by corruptions.<div eID="gen20123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... deserts--</hi>where there is nothing to eat; whence the foxes become so ravenous and crafty in their devices to get food. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11163"/><div sID="gen20125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11163"/><hi type="bold">5. not gone up into ... gaps--</hi>metaphor from breaches made in a wall, to which the defenders ought to betake themselves in order to repel the entrance of the foe. The breach is that made in the theocracy through the nation's sin; and, unless it be made up, the vengeance of God will break in through it. Those who would advise the people to repentance are the restorers of the breach (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.30">Eze 22:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Psa 106:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.30">30</reference>).<div eID="gen20125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hedge--</hi>the law of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.12">Psa 80:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Is 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">5</reference>); by violating it, the people stripped themselves of the fence of God's protection and lay exposed to the foe. The false prophets did not try to repair the evil by bringing back the people to the law with good counsels, or by checking the bad with reproofs. These two duties answer to the double office of defenders in case of a breach made in a wall: (1) To repair the breach from within; (2) To oppose the foe from without.<div eID="gen20126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to stand--</hi>that is, that the city may "stand."<div eID="gen20127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... day of ... Lord--</hi>In the day of the battle which God wages against Israel for their sins, ye do not try to stay God's vengeance by prayers, and by leading the nation to repentance. <div eID="gen20128" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11168"/><div sID="gen20141" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11168"/><hi type="bold">11. overflowing--</hi>inundating; such as will at once wash away the mere clay mortar. The three most destructive agents shall co-operate against the wall--wind, rain, and hailstones. These last in the East are more out of the regular course of nature and are therefore often particularly specified as the instruments of God's displeasure against His foes (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.18">Ex 9:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.10.11">Jos 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.22">Job 38:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.2">Is 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">30:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.21">Re 16:21</reference>). The Hebrew here is, literally, "stones of ice." They fall in Palestine at times an inch thick with a destructive velocity. The personification heightens the vivid effect, "O ye hail stones." The Chaldeans will be the violent agency whereby God will unmask and refute them, overthrowing their edifice of lies. <div eID="gen20141" type="x-p"/>

Perhaps they made their dupes rest on these cushions in a fancied state of ecstasy after they had made them at first stand (whence the expression, "every stature," is used for "men of every age"). As the men are said to have built a wall (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">Eze 13:10</reference>), so the women are said to sew pillows, &c., both alike typifying the "peace" they promised the impenitent.<div eID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make kerchiefs--</hi>magical veils, which they put over the heads of those consulting them, as if to fit them for receiving a response, that they might be rapt in spiritual trance above the world.<div eID="gen20150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head of every stature--</hi>"men of every age," old and young, great and small, if only these had pay to offer them.<div eID="gen20151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hunt souls--</hi>eagerly trying to allure them to the love of yourselves (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.26">Pr 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2Pe 2:14</reference>), so as unwarily to become your prey.<div eID="gen20152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will ye save ... souls ... that come unto you--</hi>Will ye haul after souls, and when they are yours ("come unto you"), will ye promise them life?
